text:
On Project Systems and Toolkits, pick the main system, and tick any other systems on the same job.
Each one brings its own toolkit: a plan, install steps, tests, repairs and the tools you need.
The systems you pick turn on the tools the job needs, and put those systems first on Installation, Service, Troubleshooting and the Specifications Library.

Find Location and Auto-Plan takes an address or G P S coordinates, and shows the spot on a map and in [3D](/θɹˌi dˈi/), with its ground height.
Tap Build plan for this location, and the app looks over the terrain for a good tower spot nearby, and sets up the sites for you to review.
The plan fills in Site Data, the equipment, the coverage run, the path profile, the materials list, the code checks and the test plan, so every later page has a starting point.

Site Data and G P S holds each site: its G P S position, ground height, structure and antenna height.
It shows the distance and [azimuth](/ˈæzəməθ/) between sites, and the magnetic declination.
Use this device's G P S, or bring in a G P S log.
Every map, path profile and coverage run, the F C C search, and the weather and magnetic pages use these sites.
Runs measured between sites go to the Materials list.

Section two is the site survey.
On Field Notes and Photos, write a note, add photos from the camera, and save your G P S position.
The site survey checklist keeps track of what to look at while you are there.
Notes link to a site, sync with the project, and print in Reports.
The Troubleshooting Wizard and the Weather page can add notes here too.

On [Live](/lˈIv/) Signal Readings, connect a signal meter by Bluetooth, a U S B cable or Wi-Fi, or use the phone's own signal.
The big number is the reading right now.
It uses the meters connected on Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Devices, and its results feed Drive Test and Calibration and the Emergency Radio page.

Section three is low-voltage design.
On Auto-Design, describe the building: its type, floors and size.
The app recommends the devices for each system, lays them out, and shows them on a [2D](/tˌu dˈi/) plan and a [3D](/θɹˌi dˈi/) model.
Its layout feeds the [2D](/tˌu dˈi/) and [3D](/θɹˌi dˈi/) models, the campus plan, the Materials list, the Fire Alarm and Emergency Radio pages, and Blueprints, so you describe the building once.

Emergency Radio, for [ERCES](/ˈɜɹsiz/) and [BDA](/bˌidˌiˈA/) systems, works out the donor signal, the [BDA](/bˌidˌiˈA/) gain, and the downlink budget to the worst spot in the building, with the code checks for the I F C and [NFPA](/ˌɛnˌɛfpˌiˈA/) twelve twenty-five.
It takes the county's public-safety channels from Radio Reference, the donor tower from F C C Towers, and the measured coverage from [Live](/lˈIv/) Signal Readings.

Solar and DC Power sizes a remote site: the loads, the battery bank, the solar panels, and the wire sizes, using the worst month of sun for your location.
Its equipment goes to the Materials list, and the Weather page warns you when the forecast low is colder than the design record low.

Grounding and Structure covers ground rods, bonding and the ground ring, with a live code check, and the structure loading for the tower or mast.
Its lines go to the Materials list, and the Installation Guides cover antenna feedline and grounding step by step.

F C C Towers and Licenses.
Pick a project site, an address or your G P S, and the app lists every F C C registered tower and licensed transmitter nearby.
The F C C data for North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Tennessee and Virginia is built in, so it works with no internet.
From here, add a tower as a site, aim the emergency radio donor antenna at it, or send it to the [FAA](/ˌɛfˌAˈA/) Height Check.

Path Profile shows the ground between two sites, with the earth's curve, the line of sight and the [Fresnel](/fɹənˈɛl/) zone, and tells you if the path is clear.
It uses the sites from Site Data and the terrain from Map and Terrain.

Coverage Prediction paints a signal heat map over the terrain, and checks it against your acceptance criteria, for mobile, portable and in-building coverage.
It uses the Equipment settings and the terrain.
Drive Test calibration tunes it, and its signal map feeds Multi-site, Scenarios and the Photo Site Survey.

On Tilt, [Azimuth](/ˈæzəməθ/) and Power, the side view follows the real ground along the antenna's [azimuth](/ˈæzəməθ/), and shows where the main beam and its edges come down.
The ground is colored by the predicted signal.
It uses the antenna from Equipment and the predicted signal from Coverage Prediction.

Blueprints and Drawing Sets turns the design into a drawing set for the permit, with a north arrow and the device layout.
It is drawn from the Auto-Design layout, with the codes from Code Compliance, the fire alarm battery calculation, and a north arrow that uses the magnetic declination.

Section six is equipment and materials.
The Specifications Library covers every low-voltage system.
Access control has door controllers, card readers, credentials, mag locks, electric strikes, power supplies and exit switches.
Items from it go on the Materials list, and the Troubleshooting Wizard and Service use its specifications and manuals.

The Vendors page keeps your suppliers, with the phone, email, account and terms.
Tap Add field for anything else you need.
If a vendor gives you a stock address, the app checks stock and price by itself when you are online.
Vendors are shared by every project, and appear in Search online on the Materials list.

Section ten, Reports, Proposals and Closeout.
Pick a proposal, a build plan, a site survey report or the closeout package, choose the sections, then print it, or save it as P D F, Word or Excel.
It pulls from every page: your company and the client, the materials and labor, field notes and photos, test results and the equipment list.

Now the tools, which you can open any time.
The Calculators page has calculators for cabling, power, fire alarm, sound, radio and antennas.
The [azimuth](/ˈæzəməθ/) calculator takes two G P S positions or addresses, or two project sites.
Results can be applied to the project, and Low-Voltage Principles opens the matching calculators.

Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Devices: connect a signal meter, a G P S receiver, a laser distance meter or a barcode scanner once, and every page uses it.
A laser measurement goes right into the box you tap.
The meter feeds [Live](/lˈIv/) Signal Readings, the G P S receiver feeds every G P S button, the laser fills in lengths, and the scanner feeds Asset Tags.
The checked declination and storm level are saved on the project by themselves, and used on drawings, in reports, and on synced devices.

Weather and Radar shows the latest report from the nearest National Weather Service station: temperature, feels-like, wind and gusts, humidity, pressure and visibility.
With no internet, it shows the last weather downloaded, and how long ago.

The work-day check looks at the next twenty-four hours: lightning, so no tower, roof or lift work, wind for climbing and lifts, cold for cable pulls and batteries, heat, and rain.
Below it, the next twenty-four hours show the temperature and the chance of rain.

When the weather is for the project site, it is saved on the project.
Site Data, the Installation Guides and Service then warn you about alerts, lightning, high wind, cold or heat, and Solar and DC Power checks the forecast low against the design record low.
One tap adds today's weather to Field Notes.

Sync Devices moves your projects between your phone, tablet and computer: directly over Wi-Fi by scanning a code, by Bluetooth or email, or through a cloud-drive folder.
Radio Reference data and your sign-in never sync.
